newsitem.title: MOZAMBIQUE: Mozambique's ex-rebels demand stronger role in army.
newsitem.headline: Mozambique's ex-rebels demand stronger role in army.

text.p: Mozambique's former rebel leader Afonso Dhlakama says he is through with war but considers that the merging of his ex-Renamo combatants into a single national army is incomplete.
"I don't want to go back to war. I accepted mediation, but the problem is that the process of integration has not finished," the former rebel leader told Reuters.

Renamo lost to the formerly Marxist Frelimo, which had run Mozambique since independence from Portugal in 1975, in the first democratic elections in 1994, two years after both sides signed a peace accord in Rome to end a 16-year civil war.
The U.N.-backed transition to peace included demobilising government and former rebel soldiers and integrating them into a single army, but Dhlakama said: .
"The agreement on integration has not been fulfilled. We need to create an equal balance of numbers. Frelimo has reorganised its own people in the army and police."

He said both sides agreed to incorporate 15,000 men each into a new Mozambican army, but said that just over 2,000 Renamo soldiers had been integrated into the army, whose size has slowly shrunk from 12,000.
"All the others went home," Dhlakama added in the recent interview in the Mozambican capital.
He said he planned to call a meeting of the United Nations and donor countries to insist that the matter be resolved.
"If we leave this, is can become a danger (to peace)," he said.
Renamo is officially a member of a power-sharing government, but political tensions still exist.
The military effectively does not serve any useful function, although parliament recently approved legislation allowing it to take part in peacekeeping overseas.
The army of one of the world's poorest countries is short of vehicles and soldiers, the air force is grounded and the navy lacks boats.

Recently the Renamo leader travelled to his movement's former base at Maringue, near the second city of Beira, to calm tensions between his supporters and the government's special police force, deployed with armoured vehicles after threats of demonstrations over high living costs.

"The deployment of the Rapid Intervention Police (PIR) with BTR combat vehicles scared the people who felt threatened and intimidated. Many left the area, fearing a return of the war," Dhlakama said. He denied Renamo had a small private army.
"We agreed in Rome that the a total of 150 men would be assigned to Renamo leaders as bodyguards," he said.
The Renamo leader said none of his elements had been incorporated into the PIR and people had viewed the force's presence in Maringue as hostile.
But despite political tensions Mozambique is mostly at peace, creating good conditions for increased investment coupled with economic reform measures.
"Only with foreign investment can there be stability in Mozambique," Dhlakama said.
He was critical of the government's slow pace in implementing changes on the ground.
"People want to see changes in health, education and living conditions. There is no development in the rural areas because people are coming to the cities to find jobs," he said.
Renamo's main support comes from the countryside.
